transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

I came because I don’t really feel like I’m managing it anymore. I’ll be at the church office, trying to answer emails or talk to someone like everything is normal, and then it just… hits me. Out of nowhere.

It’s the scene with my cousin on the pavement. I can see it like it’s right there again — the lights, the shouting, all of it. Sometimes it’s like I can hear it even when I know I’m standing inside the church and nothing is happening there. I’ll try to keep my face steady because I’m supposed to be calm for people, but inside I’m right back there, and it’s hard to pull myself out of it. That’s what brought me in.
How long have you been experiencing these symptoms since the event with your cousin occurred?

It’s been… since it happened, really. Since my cousin was killed. That was two years and three months ago now, and I know that sounds like a long time to still be saying it feels recent, but in my head it doesn’t feel like it’s stayed back there where it belongs.

I kept thinking at first that maybe after the funeral, or after a few months, or after I got back into my work at the church, it would start to settle. But it’s been going on this whole time — two years and three months.

latest_inference.note: The patient reported symptoms persisting for over two years, which meets the criteria for chronic post-traumatic stress disorder.
